**“Follow thy fair sun, unhappy shadow”**

Follow thy fair sun, unhappy shadow,  
Though thou be black as night,  
And she made all of light,  
Yet follow thy fair sun, unhappy shadow.

Follow her whose light thy light depriveth,  
Though here thou liv’st disgraced,  
And she in heaven is placed,  
Yet follow her whose light the world reviveth.

Follow those pure beams whose beauty burneth,

Pursue your beautiful sun, sorrowful shadow.  
Even though you are dark like the night,  
and she is formed entirely of light,  
continue after your radiant sun, unhappy shadow.

Go after the one whose brightness takes away your own.  
Although you live here in shame,  
while she has a place in heaven,  
still follow the one whose light restores life to the world.

Chase those spotless rays whose beauty blazes.  
They have burned you so deeply  
that you must remain black,  
until her gentle beams change your darkness into brightness.

Keep following her while her splendor still shines.  
A cruel night will one day arrive  
and weaken all of her light,  
and this is what the dark, miserable shade foresees.

Continue to follow, since destiny has ordered it so.  
The Sun must always have its shadow,  
until both disappear together:  
the Sun still honored, and the shadow still rejected.

outputs.L3:
The poem presents a speaker who urges the “unhappy shadow” to continue following the bright, radiant “sun,” even though the shadow itself is dark, disgraced, and seemingly worthless by comparison. The contrast between the two figures is central: the sun shines with beauty and power, while the shadow exists only as a dark and diminished reflection. Yet despite its lowly condition, the shadow is drawn irresistibly toward the sun and cannot help but follow it.

The “sun” represents the beloved, a figure whose beauty and presence give life and light to the world. She is described as radiant and life-giving, like the sun itself. However, her brilliance has a painful effect on the speaker or “shadow.” While she illuminates everything around her, she also deprives the shadow of any brightness of its own. In her presence, the shadow becomes even more aware of its darkness and inferiority.

The shadow has been scorched and darkened by the beloved’s beauty. Her radiance is so intense that it has burned rather than healed, leaving the shadow marked by suffering and disgrace. Even so, the shadow still hopes that the beloved’s kindness may one day transform its darkness into light. There is a longing for mercy and redemption: if her beauty has the power to wound, perhaps her compassion has the power to restore.

At the same time, the poem introduces a warning. The beloved’s glory, though dazzling, will not last forever. A “luckless night” will eventually come and dim her light, reminding her that even the brightest beauty is subject to time, change, and death. The sun may seem eternal in its brilliance, but it too must set.

In the end, the shadow is fated to follow the sun until both vanish. The beloved, like the sun, will be honored for her radiance, while the shadow will remain despised and overlooked. Their destinies are linked, yet unequal: the sun is admired for its glory, and the shadow is condemned for its darkness. The poem therefore reflects on love, beauty, suffering, and mortality, showing how devotion can persist even when it brings humiliation and pain.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents unrequited devotion through the extended metaphor of an “unhappy shadow” that follows a brilliant and unattainable “sun.” The shadow represents the speaker or lover, while the sun represents the beloved: radiant, powerful, and distant. Although the shadow is drawn irresistibly toward the sun, it can never truly possess or equal it. Instead, the sun’s brightness only makes the shadow’s own darkness more visible. In this way, the poem transforms love into a painful condition in which admiration and suffering are inseparable.

Throughout the poem, the shadow’s devotion is marked by humiliation and loss. It is “darkened,” “disgraced,” and “diminished” by the very light it worships. This suggests that the beloved’s greatness does not comfort the speaker but instead emphasizes his weakness and dependence. The shadow has no independent existence; it appears only because of the sun and is defined by its relationship to her. Even when the beloved’s light harms or lowers him, the shadow continues to follow. His love is therefore not presented as a free or joyful choice, but as a fate he cannot escape.

The metaphor also highlights the inequality between the lover and the beloved. The sun is elevated, luminous, and commanding, while the shadow is low, dark, and powerless. Their relationship is one-sided: the shadow is completely devoted, but the sun remains distant and unchanged. This imbalance captures the emotional pain of loving someone who does not return that love in the same way. The speaker’s devotion may be constant, but it brings no reward beyond continued attachment.

By the end of the poem, the shadow’s fate is clear. It must remain inseparable from the sun until both finally fade. This conclusion gives the poem a sense of inevitability, as if the lover’s suffering is bound to continue for as long as the beloved exists. The shadow cannot abandon the sun, even though following her causes shame and diminishment. The poem therefore emphasizes the persistence of unequal love: a love that endures not because it is happy or fulfilled, but because it has become part of the lover’s very being.

## “Follow thy fair sun, unhappy shadow”  
**Thomas Campion**

Follow thy fair sun, unhappy shadow,  
Though thou be black as night,  
And she made all of light,  
Yet follow thy fair sun, unhappy shadow.

Follow her whose light thy light depriveth,  
Though here thou liv’st disgraced,  
And she in heaven is placed,  
Yet follow her whose light the world reviveth.

Follow those pure beams, whose beauty burneth,  
That so have scorched thee  
As thou still black must be  
Till her kind beams thy black to brightness turneth.

Follow her, while yet her glory shineth;  
There comes a luckless night  
That will dim all her light;  
And this the black unhappy shade divineth.

Follow still, since so thy fates ordained;  
The sun must have his shade,  
Till both at once do fade,  
The sun still proved, the shadow still disdained.

## Anthology note summary

Thomas Campion was an English poet, composer, and physician, especially known for writing lyric poems meant to be sung. This poem uses the image of a shadow following the sun to describe unrequited or unequal love: the “shadow” is dark, dependent, and scorned, while the beloved is radiant and elevated like the sun. The repeated command to “follow” emphasizes devotion despite rejection or hopelessness.
